lead: A UPS keeps a load alive when the mains fails. Mains normally feeds a rectifier or charger, which holds a DC bus with a battery. An inverter turns that DC into AC for the load. In the on-line type the load always runs from the inverter, so a mains failure is invisible. UPS systems protect computers, hospital monitors, telecom towers, railway signalling and payment servers. This chapter compares off-line, line-interactive and on-line UPS topologies, explains transfer time, VA rating versus watts, output waveform quality, and battery sizing for a required backup time.
prereq: You need: Unit 3 for the charger stage and switched-mode power supplies, and Unit 4 for the full-bridge inverter and sinusoidal PWM; charger details are in 6.2.

blocks.text: An off-line UPS, also called standby, leaves the load on the mains in normal operation. The charger keeps the battery full and the inverter is off. When mains fails, a static transfer switch moves the load to the inverter. Transfer time is typically 4 to 10 ms. Some syllabi call this the standby type.

A line-interactive UPS adds a tap-changing transformer or buck-boost converter that corrects mains voltage while the load stays on the mains. The same inverter/charger charges the battery when mains is present. On mains failure it also switches the load to the inverter, with a transfer time of a few milliseconds, shorter than the off-line type because the inverter is already running and regulating. An on-line UPS, also called double conversion, rectifies the mains to a DC bus, holds a battery on that bus, and runs an inverter continuously into the load. The load never sees the mains directly. Mains failure changes the DC bus source from the charger to the battery, so there is no transfer time.

A static bypass is a fast switch, usually thyristors, from mains to load for inverter overload or fault. A maintenance bypass isolates the UPS for service. Ferro-resonant and rotary UPS exist for special cases; most data-centre UPS are on-line.

sections.h3: VA rating, waveform and battery sizing

blocks.text: UPS rating is in VA because inverter and transformer heating depends on current, and load current depends on apparent power S. Real power P = S × cos φ, where φ is the load power factor. A 1 kVA UPS with a 0.8 PF load can supply 800 W; with a 0.6 PF load it can supply only 600 W. Output THD = √(V₂² + V₃² + V₄² + …) ÷ V₁ × 100%, where V₁ is the fundamental RMS voltage and V₂, V₃, … are the harmonic RMS voltages. Below 3% is good for sensitive loads. Crest factor is peak value divided by RMS value. SMPS loads draw narrow pulses with high crest factor, so a UPS must supply that peak current without clipping.
S = P / cos φ; P_dc = P / η; E = V_bat × Ah × DoD; t = E / P_dc
blocks.where: S is apparent power in VA; P is real load power in W; cos φ is load power factor; P_dc is battery-side DC power in W; η is inverter efficiency; V_bat is nominal battery voltage in V; Ah is battery capacity in ampere-hours; DoD is depth of discharge as a fraction; E is usable energy in Wh; t is backup time in hours.

blocks.text: Battery sizing uses usable energy, not the printed Ah alone. The charger must also replace the energy taken during an outage. Ageing, low temperature and high discharge current reduce the delivered Ah, so field designs add margin. For grid-tied battery interfaces, see 6.6.

A linear supply steps down and rectifies the mains, then drops the excess voltage across a series transistor; it is clean but bulky and low efficiency. An SMPS chops at high frequency, so it is small and efficient, but it draws pulsed current with high crest factor and injects harmonics. That crest factor is what matters for UPS sizing: the UPS must supply the peak current of the SMPS load without clipping or tripping. A UPS is an AC power supply with stored energy. It also acts as a power conditioner, regulating voltage, filtering spikes and holding frequency. A power conditioner may only filter and regulate, with no battery. Choose UPS VA from load VA, not watts alone, and add margin for startup.

spec.title: On-line UPS
spec.aria: Mains feeds a rectifier that holds a DC bus with a battery; an inverter feeds the load, and a static bypass can join the load straight to the mains.

examples.question: A 1 kVA on-line UPS feeds a 640 W load at 0.8 lagging power factor. The battery is 48 V, 100 Ah, the inverter efficiency is 90%, and the battery may be taken down to 80% of its capacity. Find the DC current drawn from the battery and the backup time.
steps: Load apparent power: S = P / cos φ = 640 / 0.8 = 800 VA. The 1 kVA UPS rating is greater than 800 VA, so the load fits.
Inverter DC power: P_dc = P / η = 640 / 0.9 = 711.1 W.
Battery DC current: I = P_dc / V_bat = 711.1 / 48 = 14.8 A.
Usable battery energy: E = V_bat × Ah × DoD = 48 × 100 × 0.8 = 3840 Wh.
Backup time: t = E / P_dc = 3840 / 711.1 = 5.4 h.
examples.answer: The battery supplies about 14.8 A at 48 V, and the usable energy gives about 5.4 hours of backup.

traps: Multiplying VA by hours and calling it stored energy. Apparent power must pass through the load power factor and the inverter efficiency before it becomes battery watts.
Using battery Ah × voltage as backup time without depth of discharge and inverter efficiency. A 100 Ah battery is not 100 Ah of usable energy.
Choosing a UPS only by watts. The UPS VA rating must exceed load VA, because current heats the inverter and transformer.
Thinking every UPS has the same transfer time. Off-line and line-interactive types switch the load; on-line double conversion does not transfer the load on mains failure.
Ignoring crest factor. A low-THD UPS can still trip on an SMPS load that draws high peak current.

quiz.a: An uninterruptible power supply is an AC backup system with a charger, a battery and an inverter. It feeds the load when mains fails.

quiz.q: Why does an on-line UPS have no transfer time on mains failure?
quiz.a: The load always runs from the inverter. Mains failure only changes the DC bus source from the charger to the battery, so the output AC does not switch path.

quiz.q: A 1500 VA UPS feeds a 900 W load at 0.75 power factor. Is the load within the VA rating?
quiz.a: S = P / cos φ = 900 / 0.75 = 1200 VA. 1200 VA is less than 1500 VA, so the load is within rating, with 300 VA margin.

quiz.q: A 48 V, 100 Ah battery is used to 80% depth of discharge. Inverter efficiency is 90% and the load is 500 W. Find the backup time.
Why can a 1000 VA UPS trip on a 600 W SMPS load?
quiz.a: The SMPS draws current in narrow peaks, so its crest factor is high and its RMS current may exceed the sine-wave rating. The UPS must supply the peak current, and protection may trip even when average watts look small.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a static bypass and a maintenance bypass?
quiz.a: A static bypass automatically connects the load to mains during inverter overload or fault. A maintenance bypass is a manual path that isolates the UPS so it can be serviced.

quiz.q: A battery falls from 48 V to 42 V near the end of discharge while supplying the same load. What happens to battery current?
quiz.a: For the same DC power, I = P_dc / V_bat. At 42 V the current is 48/42 = 1.14 times the current at 48 V, about 14% higher. More current means more internal loss and a faster voltage fall.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern UPS designs use lithium-ion batteries, high-efficiency SiC inverters, modular parallel units and grid-interactive operation. Data-centre UPS may coordinate with generators, solar and battery storage. Search next for double conversion UPS, static transfer switch, depth of discharge and IEC 62040.
